title: Denis (9 October)
hook: a stone bishop in Paris holds his own head in his hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bruno, and the Carthusians in their silent valley. Your line was the cross stands while the world turns. What did you keep still? Day one thousand thirty-four.
screen: `THE CROSS STANDS WHILE THE WORLD TURNS.`

segments.voice: On the front of Notre-Dame in Paris, among the carved saints, stands a bishop in his robes. Where his head should be, there's nothing. His head is in his hands, held out in front of him, still wearing its miter. Tourists photograph him and wonder. Parisians have a story ready, and it starts on a hill at the edge of their city, where the white church of Sacré-Cœur stands now. Today, Denis.
screen: `A STONE BISHOP AT NOTRE-DAME.` → `HIS HEAD IN HIS HANDS.` → `A HILL AT THE EDGE OF PARIS.`

segments.voice: Start with an early layer of the story, from Gregory of Tours, a bishop who wrote a history of the Franks. He says Denis was sent to Gaul, to the town that would become Paris, as its bishop, and that he died by the sword for Christ. Other old accounts fill in more: he preached, people came to faith, and in a time of persecution he was arrested with two companions, a priest named Rusticus and a deacon named Eleutherius, and all three were beheaded. That's the core the Church keeps on his feast: Denis and companions, martyrs. Then the legend grew. Later tellings say that after Denis was beheaded on the hill, he stood up, picked up his own head, and walked away, preaching as he went, until he reached the place where he wanted to be buried. That's the bishop on the front of Notre-Dame. It's a story people tell, not a record. Some read it as a picture of how Parisians felt: their bishop was not finished by a sword. And the hill? Tradition reads its name, Montmartre, as the mountain of martyrs, for Denis and his companions. Historians debate where the name really comes from, but the story stuck to the place. There's one more twist. In Acts, when Paul preaches in Athens, among those who believe is a man named Dionysius the Areopagite. Medieval writers decided that Dionysius and Denis were the same man, Paul's convert sailing to Paris. Today the Church treats them as two different saints. Same name, different men, mixed together by people who loved them both.
screen: `SENT TO GAUL AS BISHOP.` · `BEHEADED WITH HIS TWO COMPANIONS.` · `THE LEGEND: HE CARRIED HIS HEAD.` · `NOT THE MAN PAUL MET IN ATHENS.` · then, large: `MONTMARTRE: THE MOUNTAIN OF MARTYRS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for France. Let your breath settle. Bring to mind France: Paris and its old churches, small villages with a bell tower in the center, and people of every faith and none who live there now. If you know someone French, start with them. If you pray, you can ask Denis, the bishop on the hill, to pray for the country he served. If you don't, simply hold its people in mind with good will. The bell holds the time.
Denis. Tradition calls him Paris's first bishop, beheaded with his companions on the hill the legend says he walked down, carrying his head.
Your line: the mountain of martyrs. Today, when you pass an ordinary place, ask what happened there before you, and who might still remember. Day one thousand thirty-four.

howItsDone: Saint Denis and companions are remembered on 9 October; in France, and especially in Paris and at the basilica of Saint-Denis north of the city, the feast is kept with Mass.

fork.setup: you're a medieval writer. two saints are named Dionysius: Paul's convert in Athens and the bishop of Paris. what do you decide?
fork.reveal: medieval writers merged them into one man; today the Church treats them as two different saints.

trapdoor: what you thought: a headless statue on a famous cathedral.
what it means: Paris's early bishop, martyred with two companions on the hill tradition names for martyrs.
what a scholar hears: Gregory of Tours gives an early account; the head-carrying legend and the merger with Dionysius the Areopagite came later.

notes: The headless bishop statue on Notre-Dame's west facade (Portal of the Virgin): confirm it is Denis and that it wears a miter.
Sacré-Cœur standing on Montmartre: confirm 'where the white church stands now' is fine.
'An early layer of the story, from Gregory of Tours': confirm and the book reference (Book 1, ch. 30).
'Their first bishop' and the word segment's 'remembered as the first bishop of Paris': based on tradition and the index hook; confirm.
Montmartre as 'mountain of martyrs' is the traditional reading; alternative derivations (Mars, Mercury) are noted only as 'historians debate'. Confirm.
'Today the Church treats them as two different saints': Dionysius the Areopagite has his own commemoration (3 October in the Martyrology); confirm.
Acts 17:34 paraphrased; 'among those who believe' summarizes the verse. Confirm or soften.

Editor: Gregory of Tours (History 1.30) gives only the mission to Paris and death by the sword, so the companions and beheading are now attributed to 'other old accounts', and 'sent from Rome' became 'sent to Gaul'; 'the history the Church keeps' became 'the core'; cut the stock 'every hill has a story' from the carry; match pair reworded.
Audit: narrator line 'it says something true about how Parisians felt' reframed as 'some read it as'. Facts re-checked; no other changes.
